question: How can bootstrap replications be turned automatically into accurate, transformation-invariant confidence intervals?
hypothesis: If a monotone transformation to normality exists (with bias z0 and acceleration a), BCa intervals are second-order accurate and Fisher-correct.
contributions: Four increasingly accurate bootstrap interval algorithms: standard, percentile, BC, BCa
Second-order accuracy explained as O(1/n) coverage error versus O(1/sqrt n)
Bootstrap-t intervals, confidence densities and links to objective-Bayes (Jeffreys) intervals

results.claim: Coverage error of standard intervals is O(1/sqrt n), so quadrupling n only halves the error; second-order accurate methods (BCa) have error O(1/n).

results.claim: Percentile and BC are not second-order accurate; BCa needs all three corrections (non-normality, bias z0, acceleration a) and reduces to BC when a=0, percentile when z0=0, standard when the bootstrap histogram is normal.

results.claim: Percentile confidence density equals the bootstrap density; BCa confidence density reweights it by w(theta) (eq 11.68) with discrete weights W_b (eq 11.69).

limits: Percentile/BC/BCa rely on the existence (not knowledge) of a normalising transformation; BC and BCa work dependably only for |z0| and |a| small, say at most 0.2.
BCa needs the acceleration a, which is not a function of the bootstrap distribution and is computed separately (jackknife, abc, accel); it needs B around 2000.
BC/BCa degrade with many nuisance parameters (high-dimensional MLE bias).
Bootstrap-t is not transformation invariant and needs a formula for the standard error.
Bootstrap intervals are neither exact nor optimal; the Jeffreys prior is not truly uninformative in multiparameter problems.
Eigenratio data and figures 10.2, 10.6 come from Chapter 10 and are not reprinted.
practices: Use the percentile method as a transformation-invariant 'automatic Fisher' in place of the standard interval; B about 2000 (sec 11.2).
Compute z0 = Phi^-1(p0) with p0 = fraction of replications below theta-hat even if BC/BCa is not used, as a warning of dangerous bias (sec 11.4).
Prefer BCa for second-order accuracy; if a is unavailable BC is a reasonable choice (note 6).
Use B about 2000 for intervals, 200 or fewer suffices for standard errors (sec 11.4).
Be wary of BC/BCa when |z0| or |a| exceed about 0.2 (sec 11.4).
Apply bootstrap-t on a sensible scale (e.g. Fisher z) and only when a se formula exists (sec 11.5).
